fields.ou_involvement: Mars Express carried the OU-led Beagle 2 lander. John Murray (OU) was a co-investigator on the orbiter’s instrument teams (HRSC camera), per ESA’s payload documentation.

candidates.name: WSO-UVS (Spektr-UF)
candidates.why: Listed as a current CEI mission.

fields.description: A Russian-led ultraviolet space observatory for 115–310 nm, with Spain and Japan as partners.
fields.ou_involvement: The Centre for Electronic Imaging studies radiation damage to the CCD camera’s sensors and their ability to integrate for long periods at very low noise.

candidates.name: International Mars Ice Mapper (I-MIM)
candidates.why: The OU received £2 million, then £1.2 million, from UKSA for the imager detector. It is a significant OU instrument role.

fields.description: A proposed Canadian-led orbiter to map shallow water ice on Mars ahead of human exploration.
fields.ou_involvement: Manish Patel’s team is developing the imaging detector for a visible–infrared multispectral imager, with the University of Bern.

candidates.why: The OU’s evidence to Parliament cites OU discoveries from Apollo and Luna samples. An Apollo lander model already exists in the project’s models.

fields.ou_involvement: OU laboratories have analysed returned Apollo and Luna samples, for example water and oxygen isotopes in lunar rocks. Name specific studies before using this.

candidates.name: Schiaparelli
candidates.why: Suggested in the sheet’s "missing a mission" boxes.

fields.description: Schiaparelli was ESA's Entry, Descent and Landing Demonstrator Module, carried to Mars with the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter in 2016. It returned data throughout its descent through the Martian atmosphere, but a fault in its guidance software ended its parachute phase too early, and it crashed onto Meridiani Planum on 19 October 2016.
fields.ou_involvement: The OU was part of the team behind DREAMS, Schiaparelli's suite of environmental sensors designed to measure the weather at the surface of Mars. OU scientists were also heavily involved in analysing the entry, descent and landing data to work out the state of the Martian atmosphere when it arrived.

candidates.name: I-MIM
candidates.why: Suggested in the sheet’s "missing a mission" boxes.

fields.description: The International Mars Ice Mapper (I-MIM) is a proposed orbiter, led by NASA with international partners, that would use radar to map water ice buried near the surface of Mars and help choose landing sites for future human missions.
fields.ou_involvement: The OU is leading the analysis of the CHROMA-D detector for imaging the surface of Mars on the I-MIM mission. OU researchers are characterising the detector's performance and its sensitivity to radiation, to assess how well it suits the mission.

candidates.name: AlSat-Nano
candidates.why: Suggested in the sheet’s "missing a mission" boxes.

fields.description: AlSat-Nano was a joint UK-Algerian mission to build and operate a 3U CubeSat, launched in 2016. The project was designed to train Algerian students, drawing on UK engineering experience.
fields.ou_involvement: The OU provided the C3D2 camera payload, based on the C3D camera flown on UKube-1. It took pictures of the Earth's surface while advancing the technology readiness of commercial camera sensors, and also monitored the CubeSat's deployable AstroTube boom.

candidates.name: DART
candidates.why: In the sheet’s suggestion boxes (name only). Simon Green was involved.

fields.orbit_type: landed (on Dimorphos, at an illustrative impact site)
fields.description: NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was the first test of planetary defence by changing an asteroid's path. Launched in November 2021, it deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos, on 26 September 2022, shortening its orbit by about 32 minutes. ESA's Hera mission was sent to study the aftermath.

candidates.name: MAGPIE
candidates.why: Added to the sheet by a colleague (rows 89).

fields.landed_coords: illustrative south-pole site, kept clear of PROSPECT and LUPEX
fields.description: MAGPIE is ESA's first lunar rover, designed to operate for up to 10 Earth days at the lunar south pole, where it will drill into the subsurface to analyse material for water and other volatiles. The rover is being built by ispace Europe and is scheduled to launch with Intuitive Machines in 2029.
fields.ou_involvement: The Open University is contracted to develop the Volatile Analyser (VA), a key element of the Lunar Volatiles Science (LVS) payload for ESA's MAGPIE rover. Building on the OU's heritage in ion-trap mass spectrometry, the instrument will analyse lunar material to identify and measure water and other volatiles, helping to characterise their abundance and how they vary with depth at the Moon's south pole.

candidates.name: Shackleton Rover
candidates.why: Added to the sheet by a colleague (row 90).

fields.landed_coords: illustrative, near Shackleton crater at the south pole
fields.description: Taking inspiration from Sir Ernest Shackleton's 1914 expedition, and in coordination with his family, Shackleton Rover is a proposed UK-led mission to the lunar south pole. It would showcase and develop the UK's technological, scientific and industrial capabilities in space exploration while inspiring the next generation of space scientists and engineers. By establishing a long-lived experiment on the Moon, it would also give the UK a voice in the responsible exploration of the Moon and its resources.
fields.ou_involvement: Open University scientists are involved in defining the payload and the mission for the Shackleton Rover, a concept for an entirely UK-built and operated rover system for the lunar south pole.

candidates.name: Itokawa
candidates.why: Ben Rider-Stokes (email): he was recently allocated Itokawa particles, and Monica Grady has studied them before.

fields.description: Itokawa is a small, peanut-shaped near-Earth asteroid about 535 metres long, named after Hideo Itokawa, the father of Japanese rocketry. In 2005 it was visited by JAXA's Hayabusa spacecraft, which in 2010 brought back the first samples ever collected from an asteroid. Its surface of boulders and gravel suggests it is a rubble pile, reassembled from the fragments of an earlier collision.
fields.ou_involvement: OU researchers have been allocated particles of Itokawa returned by Hayabusa, to study what the asteroid is made of and how it formed.

fields.orbit: hovering beside Itokawa (as Hayabusa2 at Ryugu)
fields.description: Hayabusa was a JAXA mission that launched in 2003 and reached the near-Earth asteroid Itokawa in 2005. Despite many technical setbacks, it returned a capsule containing tiny grains of the asteroid to Earth in 2010: the first asteroid samples ever brought back.
fields.ou_involvement: OU researchers study grains of Itokawa returned by Hayabusa (see Itokawa).

candidates.name: Enceladus
candidates.why: Dave Rothery (Teams): ask Rachael Hamp, who is on the team for ESA’s proposed L4 Enceladus Orbilander (2050s). Vic Pearson (email) also flagged the L4 Enceladus work as missing.

fields.orbit: from JPL mean elements: a_km 238,400, e 0.0047, rate 262.7319; Laplace plane
fields.description: Enceladus is a small, bright icy moon of Saturn, about 500 km across. Jets of water vapour and ice grains erupt from cracks near its south pole, fed by a salty ocean beneath its icy crust, and the Cassini spacecraft sampled them by flying through the plume. Its ocean contains many of the ingredients thought to be needed for life, making it a prime target in the search for habitable worlds.
fields.ou_involvement: (none yet: ask Rachael Hamp for a few words on the OU’s part in the proposed L4 Enceladus mission)
